meta.description: Compare diamond quality using the 4Cs, D–Z colour grades, FL–I3 clarity, cut, carat, polish, symmetry and fluorescence before choosing a natural diamond.

hero.title: Diamond Quality Chart: How to Compare the 4Cs
paragraphs: A diamond quality chart helps you compare cut, colour, clarity and carat weight—the four characteristics commonly known as the 4Cs.

The highest grade in every category is not automatically the best purchase for every buyer. Some differences affect visible beauty, while others mainly affect rarity and price. The correct balance depends on the diamond’s shape, size, setting, intended use and your priorities.
Use this chart to understand grading terminology, compare natural diamonds more accurately and recognise when a technically higher grade may not provide a meaningful visible advantage.

quickAnswer.title: Quick Answer: What Determines Diamond Quality?
intro: Diamond quality is primarily described using four factors:
bullets: Cut: How effectively the diamond’s proportions and workmanship interact with light
Colour: How colourless a D-to-Z diamond appears
Clarity: The relative absence of internal inclusions and external blemishes
Carat weight: How much the diamond weighs
closing: For a round brilliant diamond, cut quality normally has the greatest immediate effect on brightness, fire and scintillation. Colour and clarity affect rarity and appearance, while carat measures weight rather than visible size or beauty.

A balanced natural diamond might combine a strong cut, near-colourless appearance and clarity without eye-visible inclusions. However, no colour-and-clarity combination guarantees beauty. The individual diamond must still be checked for proportions, measurements, transparency, fluorescence and visible performance.

For eligible standard round brilliant diamonds, the GIA cut scale is:

table.caption: GIA cut grades for eligible round brilliant diamonds

afterTable: The current GIA cut grade applies to eligible standard round brilliant diamonds in the D-to-Z colour range. Standard GIA reports do not provide the same overall cut grade for every fancy shape.
For oval, pear, marquise, emerald, cushion, radiant and other fancy-shaped diamonds, evaluate:
cutChart.cutVsShapeTitle: Cut Is Not the Same as Shape
cutVsShapeParagraphs: Shape describes the diamond’s outline, such as round, oval, pear or emerald.
Cut quality describes how well that shape has been planned, proportioned, faceted, polished and finished.
A buyer can therefore choose an oval-shaped diamond, but describing it as an “Excellent-cut oval” requires care because laboratories do not all assign overall fancy-shape cut grades in the same way.

tripleExcellentClosing: Triple Excellent does not guarantee that every diamond will look identical. Different proportion combinations, transparency characteristics and face-up patterns can exist within the same grade combination.

colourChart.title: Diamond Colour Quality Chart
intro: The GIA D-to-Z colour scale measures the degree of colour in diamonds within the normal colour range.

table.caption: GIA D-to-Z diamond colour categories
rows: Little or no detectable colour under controlled grading conditions
Rare and premium-priced; differences between adjacent grades can be subtle
Slight colour may be detectable under controlled comparison
Often provides a strong balance of appearance and price
Can work well with yellow or rose-coloured metal and antique-inspired designs
More noticeable yellow, brown or grey appearance
Best selected with the finished jewellery design in mind
Clearly visible colour within the normal range
Should be chosen intentionally for appearance and budget

afterTable: This chart applies to the D-to-Z range. Natural fancy-colour diamonds use a different colour-grading approach.
colourChart.whyDTitle: Why Does the Colour Scale Begin at D?
whyDParagraphs: GIA began the scale at D to separate its system from older, inconsistent descriptions and A, B or C-based commercial terminology.
Colour grading is conducted under controlled conditions using comparison stones. Photographs, monitor settings, jewellery lighting and surrounding metal can change how colour appears.
bestColourParagraphs: D is the highest grade in the D-to-Z system, but it is not automatically the best value for every buyer.
Many buyers compare G, H or I diamonds because they can provide a near-colourless appearance at a lower price than D–F diamonds. However, the result depends on:
bestColourClosing: A colour grade should therefore be considered in context rather than selected from the letter alone.

clarityChart.title: Diamond Clarity Quality Chart
intro: Clarity evaluates internal characteristics called inclusions and external characteristics called blemishes.
The GIA clarity scale contains 11 grades:

table.caption: GIA diamond clarity grades
rows: No inclusions or blemishes visible to a skilled grader at 10× magnification
Extremely rare and priced for rarity
No inclusions and only blemishes visible at 10×
High rarity; visible advantage may be limited
Minute inclusions extremely difficult to observe
Minute inclusions very difficult to observe
Premium clarity with slightly greater availability
Minor inclusions somewhat easier to observe
Often provides a balance of clarity and price
Some stones may look clean without magnification; individual inspection is essential
Eye visibility and transparency vary considerably
May affect appearance, transparency or durability
Greater risk of visible and structural effects
May materially affect transparency, brilliance and durability

closing: The grade does not describe inclusion location by itself. An inclusion beneath the table can affect appearance differently from one close to the girdle.

vs1Vs2.title: VS1 vs VS2: What Is the Difference?
intro: Both VS1 and VS2 diamonds fall within the Very Slightly Included category.

table.caption: VS1 versus VS2 clarity comparison
rows: Frequently clean-looking, but inspection is still required
Buyers seeking a balance between appearance and cost

closing: A VS1 diamond is technically higher in clarity, but this does not mean it will appear more brilliant than every VS2 diamond. Cut, transparency and inclusion type can matter more to the visible result.

For step cuts such as emerald and Asscher shapes, the large open facets can make inclusions easier to notice. A higher clarity grade may therefore be more useful than it would be in a brilliant-style cut.

eyeClean.title: What Does “Eye-Clean” Mean?
paragraphs: “Eye-clean” is an industry expression, not an official GIA clarity grade.
It usually means that inclusions are not visible without magnification under specified viewing conditions. However, sellers may use different:
askIntro: Before relying on the term, ask:
questions: From what distance was the diamond inspected?
Was it viewed face-up, from the side or both?
Were any inclusions visible near the centre?
Does the seller’s assessment apply to a person with normal unaided vision?
closing: A clarity grade and an eye-clean assessment answer different questions. The grading report should remain the technical reference.

price4cs.title: How the 4Cs Affect Diamond Price
intro: The 4Cs interact rather than operating independently.
If all other factors are equal:
equalBullets: A higher colour grade generally increases rarity and price
A higher clarity grade generally increases rarity and price
Greater carat weight generally increases price
Better cut quality can increase price and improve appearance
mid: In practice, all other factors are rarely equal.

A one-carat D/VVS1 round diamond and a one-carat G/VS2 round diamond can have different prices because of colour and clarity. However, their visible difference may be less significant to a buyer than the difference between an Excellent and a poorly performing cut.

polishSymmetry.title: Polish and Symmetry
paragraphs: Polish describes the quality of the diamond’s facet surfaces after cutting.
Symmetry evaluates the precision of the diamond’s shape, facet alignment and arrangement.
The common GIA finish scale includes:
closing: For many centre diamonds, Excellent or Very Good polish and symmetry provide a practical starting point.

A standard round brilliant can still receive an Excellent GIA cut grade with Very Good polish or symmetry. Triple Excellent is therefore a specific grade combination, not the minimum requirement for an attractive diamond.
Fancy shapes should also be examined for outline symmetry. A grading-report symmetry result does not replace checking whether an oval, pear, marquise or cushion looks visually balanced.

fluorescence.title: Diamond Fluorescence
intro: Fluorescence describes a diamond’s reaction when exposed to long-wave ultraviolet radiation.
GIA reports use the following strength descriptions:
mid: Fluorescence is not one of the 4Cs and is not automatically good or bad.
It should be evaluated in the individual diamond because its commercial and visual relevance can depend on:
closing: GIA research found that approximately 25%–35% of diamonds submitted for grading displayed some degree of fluorescence. Most fluorescent diamonds showed blue fluorescence.
Do not assume that every strongly fluorescent diamond is hazy. Inspect transparency and appearance rather than rejecting or accepting the diamond from the fluorescence description alone.

beyond4cs.title: Factors Beyond the 4Cs
intro: The 4Cs are the foundation of comparison, but professional selection also considers:

subsections.title: Measurements and Face-Up Spread
paragraphs: Measurements show how large the diamond appears from above and whether its dimensions suit the intended setting.
A deeply cut diamond may retain more weight below the girdle and appear smaller than another diamond of equal carat weight.

subsections.title: Proportions
paragraphs: Table size, total depth, crown angle, pavilion angle, girdle and culet can affect appearance, durability and weight distribution.
Proportion numbers should be interpreted together rather than judged from a single percentage.

subsections.title: Transparency
paragraphs: A diamond can have a strong clarity grade but still appear less crisp because of transparency or light-scattering characteristics.
Transparency must be checked through suitable images, video or physical inspection.

subsections.title: Inclusion Type and Position
paragraphs: A small central dark inclusion may be more distracting than a similarly sized inclusion near the edge. An inclusion extending to the surface or positioned at a vulnerable point may also require closer durability assessment.

subsections.title: Bow-Tie Effect
paragraphs: Oval, pear, marquise and some other elongated shapes can show a dark bow-tie pattern. A bow tie is not automatically unacceptable, but its strength and persistence should be inspected.

subsections.title: Treatments
paragraphs: Some natural diamonds receive treatments intended to alter colour or apparent clarity. Treatments should be disclosed and documented.

subsections.title: Grading Laboratory
paragraphs: Reports from different laboratories should not be assumed to be interchangeable. Confirm the grading system used and verify the report through the issuing laboratory.

goodQuality.title: What Is a Good Diamond Quality?
intro: There is no single specification that is correct for every buyer.
For a round brilliant natural diamond, a practical comparison can begin with:
bullets: VS2 or carefully evaluated SI1 clarity
Measurements appropriate for the carat weight
closing: This is not a universal recommendation. A D/VVS diamond may be appropriate for a buyer who prioritises rarity. A warmer diamond may suit a yellow-gold design. A step-cut diamond may require a different clarity balance from a round brilliant.
The right quality is the combination that delivers the desired appearance, documentation and rarity without paying for grades that do not support the buyer’s priorities.

readReport.title: How to Read a Diamond Grading Report
intro: Before purchasing, locate and verify:
closing: Enter the report number into the issuing laboratory’s official report-checking service. Confirm that the online details correspond with the document and the offered diamond.
A grading report is not normally a valuation, price guarantee or complete proof of mining origin.

checklist.title: Diamond Quality Buying Checklist
intro: Before choosing a natural diamond:
items: Confirm that the offered stone is identified as a natural diamond.
Verify the report through the laboratory.
Compare all four Cs rather than one grade.
Check millimetre measurements and face-up spread.
Review the inclusion plot and actual magnified media.
Ask whether the diamond appears clean without magnification.
Assess fancy-shape outline and bow tie where applicable.
Check the laser inscription where applicable.
Compare the complete price and commercial terms.
Keep the report, invoice and sourcing documents together.

items.question: What are the 4Cs of diamond quality?
items.answer: The 4Cs are cut, colour, clarity and carat weight. Together they provide a standard framework for describing and comparing diamond quality.

items.question: What is the best diamond quality?
items.answer: There is no single best specification for every buyer. The best choice balances visible appearance, rarity, documentation, intended setting and budget.

items.question: What is a good diamond colour and clarity?
items.answer: G–J colour with VS2 or carefully evaluated SI1 clarity can provide a useful starting point for many buyers. The appropriate combination depends on shape, size, setting and personal preference.

items.question: Is VS1 better than VS2?
items.answer: VS1 is a higher technical clarity grade than VS2. However, many diamonds in both grades appear clean without magnification, so the visible difference may be limited.

items.question: Is VS2 clarity good?
items.answer: VS2 can provide a strong balance of appearance, rarity and price. The individual diamond must still be checked for inclusion type, position, visibility and transparency.

items.question: Is SI1 clarity eye-clean?
items.answer: Some SI1 diamonds appear clean without magnification, while others have visible inclusions. “Eye-clean” is not an official GIA grade and must be assessed for the individual diamond.

items.question: Which of the 4Cs is most important?
items.answer: Cut often has the greatest immediate effect on the visible beauty of a round brilliant diamond because it influences brightness, fire and scintillation. The other Cs still affect appearance, rarity and price.

items.question: Does a higher carat mean a better diamond?
items.answer: No. Carat measures weight, not overall beauty or quality. A smaller, well-cut diamond can appear more attractive than a larger diamond with weaker proportions.

items.question: Does GIA grade the cut of oval or pear diamonds?
items.answer: GIA’s standard overall cut grade applies to eligible standard round brilliant diamonds. Fancy shapes such as oval and pear diamonds require assessment of proportions, finish, outline and actual appearance.

items.question: Is Triple Excellent the best diamond quality?
items.answer: Triple Excellent means Excellent cut, polish and symmetry on an eligible round brilliant diamond. It is a desirable specification, but diamonds within that combination can still have different proportions and appearances.

items.question: Is diamond fluorescence bad?
items.answer: No. Fluorescence is not automatically good or bad. Its effect should be evaluated in the individual diamond under relevant lighting conditions.

items.question: Can two diamonds with identical grades look different?
items.answer: Yes. Diamonds with similar report grades can differ in measurements, proportions, inclusion location, transparency, facet pattern and visible performance.
